39169540.background: Marine omega-3s and phospholipids individually support skin barrier function. Krill oil uniquely combines EPA/DHA bound to phospholipids (mostly phosphatidylcholine), which may synergistically enhance skin health. These pilot studies tested whether 1g or 2g/day krill oil improves transepidermal water loss (TEWL), hydration and elasticity in healthy adults, and whether effects correlate with omega-3 index changes.
39169540.design: Two separate randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled dose-ranging pilot trials in healthy UK adults (TEWL >10-≤24.9 g/m2/h), conducted 2016-2017. Study 1: 1g/day krill oil vs placebo capsules (51 completers of 80 randomized, 40/40 allocated). Study 2: 2g/day krill oil vs placebo (50 completers of 80 randomized, 40/40 allocated). Duration 84 days (12 weeks), assessments at baseline, day 42, day 84. Randomization via computer-generated block allocation (1:1), no stratification. No formal power calculation reported for actual analysis (target 26/group based on assumed large effect).
39169540.findings: Omega-3 index rose significantly vs placebo in both studies (Study1: krill 4.57→5.01%, placebo stable ~6.1%, p=0.003; Study2: krill 5.43→6.85%, placebo ~5.5%, p=0.0001). Primary endpoint TEWL improved significantly with krill oil vs placebo: Study1 14.47→13.83 g/m2/h (placebo no change, p=0.315; between-group p=0.002); Study2 14.25→13.02 (larger effect, between-group p<0.001). Hydration increased more with krill oil (Study1 46.31→48.31, p=0.01 vs placebo; Study2 47.52→51.17, p<0.001). Elasticity increased more with krill oil (Study1 0.788→0.803, p<0.001; Study2 0.830→0.858, p<0.001). Linear regressions showed significant correlations between omega-3 index change and TEWL, hydration, elasticity changes (r2=0.41-0.78, all p<0.001). Effects were dose-dependent, stronger at 2g/day.
39169540.limitations: Authors note: no proper power calculation was performed (pilot/dose-finding design); baseline participant characteristics (age, BMI, sex, diet) not collected; high dropout rate (~36-38%), mainly due to difficulty swallowing capsules; dropouts not invited to withdrawal visits, precluding intention-to-treat analysis. Small per-group completer samples (21-29). Funded entirely by Aker BioMarine Human Ingredients AS, manufacturer of the krill oil tested; two authors are company employees, a notable conflict of interest.

34959789.background: n-3 PUFAs and choline may aid sports performance/recovery, but their combined effect (as in krill oil) during power training (PT)/CrossFit-type high-intensity workouts was untested. Athletes often have suboptimal HS-Omega-3 Index and choline intake, and intense exercise can deplete plasma choline and antioxidant capacity, potentially impairing muscle function and recovery.
34959789.design: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled 12-week pilot trial in 35 well-trained PT/CrossFit athletes (19 krill oil, 16 olive-oil placebo; from 36 enrolled, 1 excluded for non-compliance). Krill oil dose: 2.5 g/day (5 capsules; providing 550 mg EPA/DHA, 150 mg choline, ~1.7 mg astaxanthin) vs matched olive oil placebo capsules. Outcomes (HS-Omega-3 Index, plasma choline, total antioxidant capacity/TAC, fatty acids) measured before/after a standardized high-intensity training session, pre- and post-supplementation. COVID-19 disrupted final training-session testing in 18 additional participants (baseline blood only).
34959789.findings: HS-Omega-3 Index rose only in krill oil group (4.82→6.77%, p<0.001; placebo unchanged); ARA/EPA ratio fell from 50.72 to 13.61% (p<0.001) vs no change/increase in placebo (p<0.001 between-group). EPA, DPA, DHA increased and ARA decreased significantly with krill oil (p<0.001–0.006). Krill oil group showed significantly greater post-exercise choline recovery vs placebo (p=0.04); pre-supplementation choline fell ~7.3% pooled after exercise. TAC dropped less with krill oil (−8%, from 149.2 to 137.2) than placebo (−21%, from 179.0 to 141.5), but this group difference was not statistically significant (p=0.35). No significant differences in training load/intensity between groups.
34959789.limitations: Small pilot sample (n=35, unevenly split further for choline/TAC subanalyses, e.g., n=8–14 per session), reduced power especially for TAC (null result, p=0.35) and choline sub-analyses (n=21). COVID-19 curtailed recruitment and prevented cognitive/performance testing and additional training-session data. No direct oxidative stress biomarkers or performance outcomes measured. Funded by Aker BioMarine (krill oil manufacturer) and Cienporciennatural; three authors are Aker BioMarine employees, one is Cienporciennatural owner—clear industry conflict of interest disclosed.

34444996.background: Obesity drives white adipose tissue (WAT) and liver inflammation, worsening insulin resistance and metabolic disease. Krill oil (KrO) is rich in phospholipid-bound EPA/DHA, which can be converted to anti-inflammatory oxylipins and may antagonize arachidonic acid (ARA)-driven inflammation. Prior KrO studies were short (<12 weeks); long-term effects on tissue PUFA/oxylipin profiles and organ inflammation during obesity development were unknown.
34444996.design: Preclinical study in male Ldlr−/−.Leiden mice fed high-fat diet (HFD, 45 kcal% fat) for 28 weeks: HFD control (n=15), HFD+3% w/w KrO (Superba Boost; ~0.09 g KrO/mouse/day, providing EPA≥150mg/g, DHA≥70mg/g) (n=15), and chow reference (n=6). Diets isocaloric. Not blinded/randomized beyond baseline body-weight/glucose matching. Endpoints: body composition, plasma lipids/adipokines, tissue fatty acid/oxylipin LC-MS/MS, histology, RNA-seq pathway analysis, Western blot. One-sided t-tests/Mann-Whitney vs HFD, α=0.05.
34444996.findings: KrO did not change body weight, fat mass, eWAT mass, plasma cholesterol/triglycerides vs HFD (all null). It raised eWAT EPA 13.7-fold, DHA 3.6-fold; liver EPA 10.8-fold, DHA 2.0-fold; reduced ARA ~59% (eWAT) and ~52% (liver). KrO increased anti-inflammatory oxylipins (18-HEPE, RvE2, 14-HDHA) and suppressed pro-inflammatory ones (HETEs, PGD2, PGE2, PGF2α, TXB2) in both tissues. eWAT: reduced adipocyte size (4200 vs 5063 µm²), increased adipocyte number 1.4-fold (hyperplasia), reduced crown-like structures ~42% (14.5→lower), deactivated TNFα/CCL2 pathways. Plasma leptin AUC and adiponectin AUC improved; HOMA-IR fell from 170.2±116.3 to 92.2±46.8. Liver histology/steatosis/triglycerides unchanged (null), but inflammatory pathways (IL-1β, NF-κB/RELA) suppressed, PPARα protein increased, IκBα trend up (p=0.066).
34444996.limitations: Animal (mouse) study only, single dose/duration, no oral gavage superimposed-KrO comparator group, cannot isolate whether whole KrO, specific components, or metabolites drive effects; phospholipid vs other lipid class contributions untested. Liver histology showed no improvement despite molecular anti-inflammatory changes—an important null/dissociation. Industry co-funding: Aker BioMarine (KrO manufacturer) provided partial funding and co-authored via employees, though stated no role in analysis/decisions. n=15/group, good power for animal work but not human-generalizable; not blinded for group allocation beyond baseline matching.

33015116.background: Choline is essential for muscle function and drops during long endurance exercise, potentially limiting performance. Krill oil is rich in phosphatidylcholine, an under-studied choline source in sports nutrition. This field study tested whether pre-race krill oil supplementation could counteract choline/metabolite depletion during triathlons of varying distance.
33015116.design: 47 non-professional triathletes (35M/12F, 25-61y) from Norseman Xtreme Ironman-distance (n=39) and Oslo Olympic/Sprint-distance (n=8) triathlons were randomised to krill oil (n=24; 4g/day SuperbaBoost, providing ~316mg choline) or placebo (n=23; 4g/day mixed vegetable oil) for 5 weeks pre-race. Blood drawn pre-race, immediately post-race, and next day. Randomised, placebo-controlled; blinding not explicitly described.
33015116.findings: Serum choline fell from pre- to post-race in all races (Ironman: 16.5→10.9 µmol/L, 34% drop; regular-distance: 12.4→10.6 µmol/L, 15% drop; time effect p<0.001). Krill oil group had significantly higher overall choline (main effect p<0.001) and greater increase post-race to next day (p=0.039) than placebo; krill oil raised choline especially in regular-distance race (p=0.02) but not in already-high Ironman baseline levels. Betaine dropped similarly with exercise (p<0.001) with only marginal group effect (p=0.051). DMG did not change with exercise but was 21.4% higher on average in krill oil vs placebo (p=0.006). No significant supplement effects on arginine, methionine, creatine, cysteine, homocysteine, TMAO, or TML.
33015116.limitations: Exploratory field study, small/unequal subgroup sizes (39 vs 8), non-professional cohort, no strict dietary/food-intake control, and unclear reason for unusually high Ironman baseline choline. Authors call for more controlled dose-response trials with performance/recovery outcomes. Funded entirely by Aker BioMarine; three authors (AS, LJ, LB) are company employees, a notable conflict of interest.

31652561.background: Choline is an essential nutrient; most people don't meet intake recommendations. Bioavailability differs by source: phosphatidylcholine (as in krill oil) vs choline salts. TMAO, a gut-microbiota-derived choline/betaine metabolite, is linked to cardiovascular/renal risk. This study compared plasma kinetics of choline and metabolites (betaine, DMG, TMAO) after single doses of SuperbaBoost krill oil vs choline bitartrate, with fish oil as choline-free control.
31652561.design: Randomized, placebo-controlled, two-way cross-over pharmacokinetic study in 18 healthy adults (9M/9F), 18-65y, BMI 18-30. 12 subjects received both SuperbaBoost (8g, 572mg choline) and choline bitartrate (620mg choline) capsules in crossover with 14-day washout; 6 subjects received fish oil (6g, 1800mg EPA+DHA) as non-crossover control. Blood drawn at 0, 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8, 12, 24h. Standardized low-choline diet/meals. Not blinded to product type by design description (open-label PK study); statistical analysis blinded/independent by BioTeSys/statistician. Sponsored by Aker BioMarine.
31652561.findings: Choline AUC0-24h, AUC0-12h and Cmax were comparable between SuperbaBoost and choline bitartrate (all p>0.05), both significantly higher than fish oil; Tmax was later with SuperbaBoost (4.17h vs 2.67h, p=0.0076). Betaine Cmax higher with SuperbaBoost (22.55 vs 18.87 µmol/L, p=0.0122); AUC differences not significant (AUC0-12h p=0.0641, AUC0-24h p=0.2394). DMG showed trend-level higher AUC0-12h with SuperbaBoost (p=0.0890), not significant for AUC0-24h/Cmax. TMAO markedly lower with SuperbaBoost vs choline bitartrate: AUC0-12h 10.06 vs 104.3, AUC0-24h 25.41 vs 288.3, Cmax 2.24 vs 28.99 µmol/L (all p<0.0001). No SAEs; only minor fishy aftertaste/headache reported.
31652561.limitations: Small sample (n=12 crossover, n=6 control), single-dose acute PK design—no chronic supplementation or clinical outcome data. Sampling gaps (4-12h) may have missed true Tmax for betaine/DMG. Phosphatidylcholine plasma levels not measured, limiting mechanistic interpretation. No clear statement of blinding for product administration (open-label capsule intake). Industry-funded by Aker BioMarine (krill oil manufacturer); authors from contract research organization declare no conflicts, but funder involved in study design discussions.

24461313.background: n-3 LCPUFAs lower elevated triglycerides (TG), a CVD risk factor, typically at doses of 1-4 g/day per NHPD/EFSA guidance. Krill oil delivers EPA/DHA mainly as phospholipids (EPA:DHA ~2:1), which may improve tissue uptake and avoid the LDL-C rise sometimes seen with DHA-rich marine oils. This trial tested whether krill oil could lower TG at doses below current recommendations without raising LDL-C, in people with low habitual fish intake and borderline-high/high TG.
24461313.design: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multi-center (2 US sites) trial; 300 adults (21-79y, TG 150-499 mg/dL, low fish intake) randomized (stratified by gender) to placebo (olive oil) or krill oil 0.5, 1, 2, or 4 g/day (EPA+DHA 100-800 mg/day), 8 capsules/day, 12 weeks. 267 analyzed after exclusions (33 excluded, mainly baseline TG<150). Due to high intra-individual TG variability, krill oil groups were pooled (time/dose-independent) vs placebo for the primary TG analysis (Student's t-test); other lipids analyzed by ANOVA without pooling.
24461313.findings: Baseline TG ~232 mg/dL across groups. At 6 weeks, TG fell significantly vs baseline in 1, 2, 4 g/day groups (-18.6 to -19.9 mg/dL, p<0.05); significance was lost by 12 weeks in individual dose groups. Pooled analysis (6+12 week data, all krill oil doses) showed a placebo-adjusted 10.2% TG reduction (krill oil -6.3% vs placebo +3.9% from baseline; p=0.0389), the primary outcome. LDL-C, total cholesterol, and HDL-C showed no significant changes at 6 or 12 weeks in any group (null result), supporting no LDL-C increase. Omega-3 index rose dose-dependently (e.g., 4g group: 3.65% to 6.3% at 12 weeks) confirming compliance; placebo unchanged. No serious product-related adverse events; body weight/blood pressure unchanged.
24461313.limitations: Authors note TG measurements showed unexpectedly high intra-individual variability (underestimated in power calculation), causing loss of significance at 12 weeks per-group and necessitating an exploratory pooled analysis (acknowledged as explorative, not confirmatory). Reason for TG rebound between 6-12 weeks unclear (speculative hepatic TG hypothesis). Study funded partly by Norwegian Research Council/SkatteFUNN; authors are employees of Aker BioMarine (krill oil manufacturer) or its consultant, a notable conflict of interest. Single 12-week duration; authors call for longer studies with more repeated measurements per group.

40671417.background: Diet-induced weight loss reduces both fat mass and fat-free mass (FFM), with ~25-30% of weight loss attributable to FFM decline, potentially reducing muscle strength and metabolic health. LCn-3 PUFA supplementation may attenuate FFM loss and improve muscle function, but no prior studies examined krill oil (KO) effects on muscle function parameters during diet-induced weight loss. This trial tested KO supplementation during alternate-day fasting (ADF) on body composition, muscle function, and inflammation in adults with overweight/obesity.
40671417.design: Double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled parallel trial (NCT06001632) in 41 completers (25 women, 16 men; age 39±10y; BMI 31.1±4.2) of 52 enrolled, Glasgow UK. After 4-week supplementation lead-in, participants underwent 8-week ADF (28 fasting/28 feeding days) plus 4 capsules/day of KO (n=21; each capsule 191mg EPA, 94mg DHA, 78mg choline, 100mcg astaxanthin; total 1.14g/day LCn-3 PUFA) or vegetable oil placebo (n=20). Randomization 1:1 via independent online software; capsules blinded/labeled by independent person. Outcomes: body mass, FFM (deuterium dilution), handgrip strength (HGS), chair rising test (CRT), inflammatory markers, blood pressure; analyzed by two-way repeated-measures ANOVA.
40671417.findings: Body weight fell similarly in both groups (KO −4.6±1.4kg vs placebo −4.5±1.9kg; no group/interaction effect, p>0.05); fat mass loss also not different between groups. FFM loss was significant only in placebo (−1.2±2.0kg, p<0.05) but not KO (−0.2±0.9kg, p>0.05); time×group interaction p<0.05. HGS declined significantly in placebo (−0.9±0.7kg) but not KO (−0.2±0.5kg), interaction p<0.05. CRT time improved (shortened) in KO (−1.8±0.9s, p<0.05) but not placebo (−0.3±1.2s); interaction p<0.05. TNF-α and CRP reductions were greater in KO (−1.4±0.2pg/mL and −51.4±25ng/mL) vs placebo (−0.9±0.5 and −33.5±12.6); IL-6, insulin, glucose, HOMA-IR, TAG showed no group differences. Systolic BP fell more in KO (−9±6mmHg vs −4±4mmHg, p<0.05); diastolic BP showed no interaction. Omega-3 index rose 55±37% more in KO vs placebo.
40671417.limitations: Single RCT, modest size (n=41 completers, powered for HGS MCID of 6.5kg which was not reached), 8-week duration considered short by authors. Author-noted limitations: muscle function assessed only by HGS/CRT; D2O-based FFM measurement may be confounded by fasting-induced hydration changes; no physical activity or male/female subgroup analysis; 3-day (not 7-day) diet diaries; suboptimal protein intake may have contributed to FFM loss; dried blood spot fatty acid analysis less precise than RBC analysis. Funded by Qassim University/Saudi government PhD studentship; capsules donated free by Aker BioMarine, which had no role in design/analysis; authors declare no conflicts of interest.

35504165.background: Sarcopenia (age-related muscle loss) reduces quality of life and increases falls/hospitalisation costs. Fatty fish intake correlates with better muscle function, and prior fish oil trials (4g/day, 6 months) increased muscle volume and grip strength in older adults. Krill oil, another LCn-3 PUFA source with phospholipid-bound omega-3s plus choline/astaxanthin, had not been tested for muscle outcomes in older adults; this trial aimed to fill that gap.
35504165.design: Double-blind RCT (NCT04048096), Glasgow, healthy adults >65y, BMI<35, low exercise. 102 enrolled, 94 completed (krill: 26F/23M; control: 27F/18M). Randomised 1:1 (independent online randomisation) to krill oil 4g/day (322mg/g LCn-3 PUFA: 193mg EPA, 96mg DHA, 79mg choline/g) or matched vegetable oil placebo, for 6 months. Assessments at baseline, 6 weeks, 6 months; primary outcome knee extensor maximal torque; intention-to-treat analysis. Stopped early (target 120) due to COVID-19 lockdown.
35504165.findings: Primary outcome: knee extensor maximal torque showed significant time*group interaction (p=0.0049); 6-month treatment effect +9.3% (95%CI 2.8–15.8%) vs control. Grip strength improved +10.9% (95%CI 8.3–13.6%, p<0.0001 interaction). Vastus lateralis muscle thickness +3.5% (95%CI 2.1–4.9%). EPA +214%, DHA +36%, omega-3 index +61% (all p<0.05) confirming compliance. M-wave increased +17–25% (95%CI 12.7–38.1%) but no effect on RMS, voluntary activation, rate of torque development. No differences in SPPB (4m walk, chair rise), body fat, muscle mass (bioimpedance), glucose, insulin, lipids, CRP, or quality of life (EQ-5D).
35504165.limitations: Authors note trial stopped early (94/120 target) due to COVID-19, though still adequately powered per original sample size calculation. Participants were relatively healthy/high-functioning (ceiling effect on SPPB), limiting generalisability to frail/sarcopenic populations. No direct fish-oil comparator arm, so cannot confirm krill oil superiority. Blinding efficacy not formally assessed. Funded by Saudi government studentship; oils supplied by manufacturer (Aker Biomarine) with no role in design/analysis; authors declare no conflicts of interest.

21276269.background: Overweight/obesity is linked to elevated plasma endocannabinoids (AEA, 2-AG), which correlate with metabolic syndrome features. Prior rat studies showed krill oil (KO) downregulates the endocannabinoid system more effectively than fish oil. This human study tested whether 4-week KO, menhaden oil (MO), or olive oil (OO) supplementation alters plasma endocannabinoid levels in normo-weight, overweight, and obese subjects, since effects of n-3 PUFAs on human AEA/2-AG had not previously been studied.
21276269.design: 4-week randomized, double-blind, controlled, parallel trial at 2 US sites; 63 subjects (men/women, 35-64y, waist ≥102cm men/≥88cm women), stratified by BMI (normoweight/overweight/obese). Groups: KO n=21 (216mg/d EPA+90mg/d DHA), MO n=23 (212mg/d EPA+178mg/d DHA), OO n=19 (control), all as 2g/d (four 500mg capsules). Endpoints: plasma AEA, 2-AG, phospholipid fatty acids, metabolic syndrome parameters (BMI, waist circumference, glycemia, insulinemia).
21276269.findings: Baseline: AEA significantly higher in obese vs normoweight; 2-AG significantly higher only in overweight subjects. After 4 weeks, KO significantly decreased 2-AG only in obese subjects (n=9; p<0.05), with a non-significant downward trend in overweight; AEA unchanged by KO. MO and OO produced no significant changes in AEA or 2-AG in any BMI group. In KO-treated obese subjects, 2-AG decrease correlated with plasma phospholipid n-6/n-3 LCPUFA ratio (R2=0.55, p<0.05); no such correlation in MO/OO or other BMI groups. No changes in BMI, waist circumference, glycemia, or insulinemia occurred with any treatment.
21276269.limitations: Authors call this a pilot study; small subgroup sizes (e.g., KO obese n=9, KO overweight n=5) limit power and preclude gender-difference analysis. No visceral adiposity data collected, limiting mechanistic interpretation. Effect not accompanied by metabolic syndrome improvements, possibly due to short duration/normolipidemic sample. Randomized double-blind design is a strength. Study partly funded by Aker Biomarine ASA (KO manufacturer); two authors employed by Aker Biomarine, one a paid consultant, another received research/consulting fees from the company—notable conflicts of interest.

26666303.background: Elevated plasma TAG, low HDL and oxidative/inflammatory stress contribute to atherosclerosis risk. Krill oil, rich in phospholipid-bound EPA/DHA (ratio 1.8:1) plus astaxanthin, may offer bioavailability and antioxidant advantages over fish oil. This pilot study tested whether krill oil favorably alters lipid, lipoprotein, fatty acid, redox, inflammatory and TMAO-pathway parameters relevant to cardiovascular risk in healthy adults.
26666303.design: Single-arm, open-label 28-day pilot intervention (no placebo/blinding/randomisation described) in 18 healthy volunteers (18–36y); 17 completed analysis (15 female, 2 male; mean age 23±4, BMI 20.9). Intervention: 9 capsules/day RIMFROST Sublime krill oil, providing 832.5 mg EPA+DHA/day (60mg EPA+32.5mg DHA per capsule), for 28 days. Plasma/RBC measured at baseline and endpoint; Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, Spearman correlations.
26666303.findings: Primary lipid outcome: plasma TAG fell 12% (p=0.016); large VLDL&chylomicron particles decreased (p=0.04), TAG/HDL-C ratio improved (p<0.01). Total cholesterol rose 4% (p<0.01), driven by increased HDL-C and LDL-C (both large particles increased, p=0.04); small LDL and IDL unchanged; total-chol/HDL ratio unchanged. n-6/n-3 PUFA ratio decreased in plasma and RBC (EPA, DHA, DPA up; AA down, all p<0.001-ish). Antioxidant capacity increased (p<0.01), correlating with EPA/DBI. Thrombogenicity index decreased; atherogenicity index unchanged. Cytokines (IL-1β,IL-10,IL-17,G-CSF,TNFα) unchanged (null). Choline and betaine increased, γ-butyrobetaine increased; TMAO and carnitine unchanged (null—no adverse TMAO effect). Octanoyl-, iso-/L-valeryl- and propionylcarnitine decreased; palmitoyl- and acetylcarnitine unchanged. Minor GT increase; other safety labs unchanged.
26666303.limitations: Uncontrolled, unblinded, non-randomised pilot study with small sample (n=17, mostly young healthy females), no placebo comparator, short 28-day duration, and multiple comparisons without correction. Mechanistic links (e.g., AOC-EPA correlations) are exploratory, not causal. Funded/partly financed by Rimfrost AS, which supplied krill oil and employed two co-authors (competing interest disclosed), though company had no role in data analysis/interpretation per authors.

15656713.background: Western diets favor omega-6 over omega-3 fatty acids, promoting inflammation and dyslipidemia, a key driver of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. Krill oil delivers EPA/DHA bound to phospholipids plus antioxidants (astaxanthin, vitamins A/E), potentially improving bioavailability versus fish oil triglycerides. This trial tested whether Neptune Krill Oil could improve blood lipids more effectively than fish oil or placebo in hyperlipidemic patients.
15656713.design: 12-week, multi-center, double-blind, randomized trial in 120 patients (age 25-75, mean 51) with cholesterol 194-348 mg/dL, 30/group. Group A: krill oil 2-3 g/day (BMI-dependent); Group B: krill oil 1-1.5 g/day, then 500 mg/day maintenance for additional 90 days (n=30); Group C: fish oil 3g/day (180mg EPA/120mg DHA per g); Group D: placebo (microcrystalline cellulose). Lipids/glucose measured at baseline, 30, 90 days (180 days for Group B).
15656713.findings: Krill oil dose-dependently reduced total cholesterol 13.4-18.1%, LDL 32-39%, and raised HDL 43-59% (all p=0.000) across 1-3g doses. Triglycerides fell significantly only at 2g (-28%,p=0.025) and 3g (-27%,p=0.0228); 1g and 1.5g reductions (-11%,-12%) were non-significant. Fish oil (3g) reduced cholesterol modestly (-5.9%,p=0.000), HDL +4.2%(p=0.002), but LDL (-4.6%,p=0.141) and triglycerides (-3.2%,p=0.239) were non-significant. Placebo worsened cholesterol (+9.1%) and LDL (+13%, both p=0.000). Krill oil outperformed fish oil for glucose, LDL, and (at 2-3g) triglycerides. 500mg maintenance dose sustained/improved lipid benefits at 180 days.
15656713.limitations: Small per-arm samples (n=30), short 12-week primary endpoint (180-day data only for one subgroup, n=30), and unclear compliance/dietary control beyond "healthy diet" instruction. Mechanism of action not fully elucidated; bioavailability claims rely on animal/other studies, not this trial's direct measurements. Authors affiliated with contract research organization (JSS Medical Research); funding/sponsor (Neptune Technologies, the krill oil manufacturer) not explicitly disclosed as funding source, only as product supplier—raising potential conflict-of-interest concern. No long-term cardiovascular outcome data.

27279841.background: PUFAs (EPA/DHA) have lipid-lowering and anti-inflammatory effects. Krill oil, rich in phospholipid-bound EPA/DHA plus astaxanthin, may have higher bioavailability than standard ethyl-ester fish oil, but comparative lipid/inflammatory efficacy at differing doses was unclear.
27279841.design: Double-blind, randomized, cross-over trial in 25 non-smoking, moderately hypertriglyceridemic (TG 150–500 mg/dl), non-diabetic, non-obese adults (18-70y). After 4-wk run-in, subjects received omega-3 ethyl esters 1000 mg twice daily (2000 mg/day) vs krill oil 500 mg twice daily (1000 mg/day) for 4 weeks, then 4-wk washout, then crossed to the alternate treatment for 4 weeks. Randomization via sealed envelopes with independent statistician-generated codes; identical-appearing pills.
27279841.findings: Both treatments lowered TG vs baseline (ethyl esters −72.8 mg/dl, p=0.001; krill oil −55.7 mg/dl, p=0.003), but ethyl esters were significantly more effective (p<0.05). Only krill oil significantly raised HDL-C (+4.5 mg/dl, p=0.039) and improved non-HDL-C (−8.1, p=0.009) and ApoAI (+19.4, p=0.049) vs baseline; ethyl esters showed no significant HDL-C, non-HDL-C or ApoAI change. Both reduced hs-CRP vs baseline (ethyl esters −0.14 mg/l, p=0.030; krill oil −0.35 mg/l, p<0.001), krill oil superior (p<0.05). No differences in TC, LDL-C, ApoB, glucose, creatinine, transaminases, CPK. No dropouts/adverse events; compliance near-total.
27279841.limitations: Authors note: small sample (n=25, pilot study), short 4-week treatment periods, no plasma EPA/DHA levels measured (efficacy inferred from lab markers only), limited biomarker panel without vascular imaging (no flow-mediated dilation/pulse wave velocity). Cross-over design partly offsets small size. No conflicts of interest declared; product supplied by manufacturer (Erbozeta). Results need confirmation in larger, longer trials.

26407095.background: Krill oil is rich in n-3 PUFAs (EPA/DHA) that may modulate immune function, particularly relevant to post-exercise immune perturbations. Prior fish oil research showed increased PBMC IL-2 and NK cytotoxicity post-exercise in males; whether krill oil replicates this, and affects exercise performance, in both sexes was unknown.
26407095.design: RCT, double-blind, placebo-controlled: 19 males, 18 females (25.8±5.3y) randomised to krill oil (n=18) or placebo (n=19), 2g/day (4500mg capsules; each 500mg contained 60mg EPA, 30mg DHA, 61μg astaxanthin) for 6 weeks. Maximal exercise test and cycling time trial performed pre-supplementation; time trial repeated post. Blood sampled at rest and 0/1/3h post-exercise, measuring IL-6, TBARS, erythrocyte fatty acids, NK cytotoxicity, PBMC IL-2/4/10/17/IFNγ.
26407095.findings: Krill oil increased erythrocyte EPA (75%), DHA (21%), Omega-3 Index (27%; all P<0.05) vs no change in placebo. PBMC IL-2 (interaction P=0.02) and NK cytotoxic activity (50:1 and 25:1 ratios, both P<0.05) were significantly higher at 3h post-exercise in krill oil vs control. No group/interaction effects seen for IL-6, TBARS, IL-4, IL-10, IL-17, IFNγ. Time trial completion time (control: 80.5→84.7min; krill: 83.9→85.4min), HR and VO2 showed no time, group, or interaction effects (all P>0.05) — no performance benefit.
26407095.limitations: No blood samples taken during baseline time trial, limiting within-subject pre/post comparison of immune responses. No no-exercise control group, so exercise-related changes could partly reflect circadian variation. No direct fish-oil comparator arm. Funded by Aker Biomarine Antarctic AS (krill oil manufacturer), which provided capsules but had no role in design/analysis; authors declare this didn't affect data sharing. Randomised, double-blind design; moderate sample size (n=37).

27817918.background: Dry eye disease (DED) involves tear hyperosmolarity and inflammation; lubricant drops are only symptomatic. Dietary omega-3 EFAs may lower inflammation, but prior fish oil DED trials had high bias risk, and krill oil (phospholipid-form omega-3) had never been tested for human ocular disease. This trial compared krill oil and fish oil vs placebo for treating DED.
27817918.design: Single-site (Melbourne), randomized (1:1:1), double-masked, placebo-controlled trial in 60 adults with mild-moderate DED; 54 completed. Arms: placebo (olive oil 1500mg/day, n=17), krill oil (945mg EPA+510mg DHA/day, n=18), fish oil (1000mg EPA+500mg DHA/day, n=19), all as 5 capsules/day for 90 days, monthly visits. Primary endpoints: change in tear osmolarity and OSDI symptom score, day 1 to 90.
27817918.findings: At day 90, tear osmolarity fell significantly vs placebo with both fish oil (-19.8±3.9 mOsmol/l; P<0.001) and krill oil (-18.6±4.5; P<0.001) vs placebo (-1.5±4.4). OSDI improved significantly only with krill oil vs placebo (-18.6±2.4 vs -10.5±3.3; P=0.02); fish oil showed a non-significant trend. Both oils improved tear breakup time and bulbar redness vs placebo by day 90. Krill oil reduced tear IL-17A vs placebo (27.1±10.9 vs 46.5±30.4 pg/ml; P=0.02). No significant effects on limbal redness (individual arms), corneal/conjunctival staining (individual arms), tear volume, Schirmer test, blepharitis, MG capping, NITBUT, or other cytokines (IL-2,4,6,10, IFN-γ, TNF-α). No BCVA/IOP changes; adverse events mild, none serious.
27817918.limitations: Authors state limitations: small sample (n=60) and single-site design, described as "proof-of-principle." Post hoc pooled omega-3 analysis increases multiplicity concerns. Fish oil showed no significant symptom benefit despite osmolarity improvement, highlighting placebo-response influence on subjective OSDI. Funded by Rebecca L. Cooper Medical Foundation and University of Melbourne grant; sponsors had no role in design/conduct; no other conflicts disclosed. Authors call for larger multicenter, longer-duration trials to confirm findings.

29854443.background: Krill oil (rich in phospholipid-bound EPA/DHA plus astaxanthin) improves postexercise immune function, but its effect on muscle hypertrophy/mTOR signaling was unknown. Omega-3 PUFAs have been linked to increased muscle protein synthesis via mTOR-p70s6k activation. This pilot study tested whether krill oil stimulates mTOR signaling in vitro and augments resistance-training-induced changes in body composition/performance in trained men.
29854443.design: Two-part study. (1) In vitro: C2C12 myoblasts stimulated with krill oil-derived PC or soy-PC (10/30 µM) vs vehicle control; mTOR readout = P-p70(389)/total p70. (2) Human: randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial; 21 resistance-trained men (18-30y) randomized (11 placebo, 10 krill oil), 18 completed (9/arm). Krill oil 3g/day (Rimfrost Sublime, 963mg omega-3s, 0.54mg astaxanthin, 1.3g phospholipids) or olive oil placebo, pre-workout/with breakfast, during 8-week nonlinear periodized resistance training. Outcomes: DXA body composition, 1RM bench/leg press, perceived recovery, Stroop cognitive test, CMP/CBC/UA safety, assessed at weeks 0 and 8.
29854443.findings: In vitro: krill oil-PC significantly increased mTOR signaling vs control and soy-PC at both doses (+187% and +242%, p<0.001); soy-PC showed no effect. Human trial: significant main time effect for lean mass (p=0.021), with krill oil showing significant within-group increase (+1.4kg, +2.1%, p=0.024) vs placebo (+0.3kg, +0.5%), but no between-group difference. No group differences in fat mass, bench press (+4.2kg krill vs +3.4kg placebo), leg press (+49.0kg vs +44.3kg), or perceived recovery (both p<0.0001 main time effects, no between-group differences). Stroop completion time improved similarly in both groups (trend, p~0.085-0.087). No differences in CMP, CBC, or urinalysis markers (all p>0.05). Post hoc power analysis indicated 34-84 subjects needed to detect significant lean mass differences.
29854443.limitations: Very small pilot sample (n=9/arm completed of 21 randomized), likely underpowered per authors' own post hoc power analysis (34-84 needed). No between-group significance despite within-group lean mass gain in krill oil group. Short 8-week duration, low omega-3 dose (963mg vs 2.4-6g in prior studies) may explain lack of recovery/soreness benefits. In vitro mTOR activation not confirmed in vivo (no muscle biopsy). Funded by Rimfrost USA and NIH; several authors are employees/paid consultants of Avoca Inc. (krill oil manufacturer) with a related patent, indicating conflicts of interest. Double-blind RCT design is a strength but small size limits conclusions.

38039646.background: Evidence on krill oil (KO) effects on cardiovascular disease risk factors (CVDRFs) is inconsistent across trials. A prior meta-analysis (Ursoniu et al., 7 trials, 662 participants) suggested LDL-C/TG benefits but didn't assess body composition, glycemia, or inflammation. This updated systematic review/meta-analysis aimed to comprehensively evaluate KO's effects on lipids, blood pressure, glycemic indices, body composition, and inflammatory markers using more recent RCT data.
38039646.design: Systematic review/meta-analysis (PRISMA) of 14 RCTs (18 treatment arms), 1458 adult participants (healthy or with conditions like T2D, hypertension, hypercholesterolemia, knee osteoarthritis), from 8 countries (2009–2022). KO doses ranged 0.5–5 g/day (capsules), vs placebo/comparator oils (olive, corn, sunflower, safflower oil, mineral oil, cornstarch); duration 4–26 weeks. 7 parallel-design, 6 crossover-design studies; most double-blind, placebo-controlled. Random-effects (DerSimonian-Laird) meta-analysis; subgroup, meta-regression, sensitivity, GRADE, and publication bias analyses performed.
38039646.findings: Primary outcome (lipids): KO significantly reduced total cholesterol (WMD −4.18 mg/dL, P=0.01), LDL-C (WMD −3.76 mg/dL, P=0.006), and triglycerides (WMD −10.76 mg/dL, P=0.0005; I²=85%). No effect on HDL-C (WMD 0.12 mg/dL, P=0.84). Subgroup effects were strongest with parallel design, <8 weeks duration, BMI<28. Secondary outcomes were all null: SBP (P=0.40), DBP (P=0.09), FBG (P=0.53), insulin (P=0.85), HbA1c (P=0.93), HOMA-IR (P=0.88), body weight, BMI, waist/hip circumference (all P>0.05), and CRP (P=0.73). No significant publication bias; sensitivity analyses robust. GRADE quality: high for TC/LDL-C/HDL-C, moderate for most secondary outcomes, low for HOMA-IR. Only mild GI adverse events reported.
38039646.limitations: Authors note: heterogeneous populations (healthy, hypertensive, hypercholesterolemic, osteoarthritic) limited subgroup precision; small trial numbers for some secondary outcomes (HC, WC, insulin, HbA1c, HOMA-IR, CRP, n≤5); uncontrolled lifestyle/medication confounders; substantial unexplained heterogeneity for TG (I²=85%) despite sensitivity/meta-regression/subgroup analyses. Only 4/14 trials rated low risk of bias; most "fair quality." Funded by Guangdong provincial grants; authors declare no competing interests.

39555189.background: Krill oil is rich in EPA/DHA, palmitoleic acid and astaxanthin, and prior trials suggest benefits for lipids, cognition, joint pain and muscle strength, but effects on skeletal muscle energy metabolism and mechanisms are unclear. This study examined krill oil supplementation effects on glucose/oleic acid metabolism and leucine (protein synthesis) in cultured human myotubes, both after in vivo intervention and direct in vitro treatment.
39555189.design: Randomized clinical trial (NCT04279951): 20 adults given 1 g/day krill oil (n=9) or placebo (high-oleic sunflower oil + astaxanthin, n=11) for 7 weeks; vastus lateralis biopsies before/after yielded cultured myotubes tested for glucose, oleic acid oxidation/uptake and leucine accumulation, plus transcriptomics/proteomics. Separate in vitro experiment: myotubes from 4 donors treated with krill oil (100 or 300 µg/ml) for 24h. Blinding not specified; mixed-model/paired-t/GraphPad statistics used.
39555189.findings: In vivo krill oil increased myotube oleic acid oxidation (significant with FCCP, hyperglycemia, GW501516 conditions) vs before intervention; placebo showed no change. Glucose uptake/oxidation unaffected by either intervention (null result). Oleic acid oxidation change correlated negatively with serum LDL change (krill oil group only). Leucine accumulation increased after krill oil (not placebo), indicating enhanced protein synthesis; insulin increased leucine in both groups. In vitro krill oil (24h) increased both glucose and oleic acid uptake/oxidation. Transcriptomics: 388 genes up, 241 down (e.g., GLUT1, VLDLR up; PLTP down); proteomics: 33 up/23 down proteins including LDL-receptor upregulation. No clinical parameters (BMI, glucose, TAG, LDL, HDL) significantly changed by either intervention.
39555189.limitations: Small sample (9 krill oil, 11 placebo donors; 4 donors for in vitro dosing), single-center cell-culture based study; authors note limited donor numbers may not capture in vivo complexity, urging larger diverse cohorts. Blinding details not described. No significant systemic clinical biomarker changes despite cellular effects. Funded by EU Horizon 2020, Norwegian Diabetes Association, South-Eastern Norway Regional Health Authority; authors declare no conflicts of interest.

25884846.background: EPA/DHA in krill are mainly bound to phospholipids, whereas fish oil EPA/DHA is mainly in triglycerides. This chemical difference has been proposed to affect bioavailability, potentially favoring phospholipid-bound forms. Bioavailability of krill meal (as opposed to krill oil) had not previously been studied in humans. This trial compared acute bioavailability of EPA+DHA from krill oil, krill meal, and fish oil.
25884846.design: Randomized, single-dose, single-blind, cross-over, active-reference trial (NCT02089165) in 15 healthy Finnish adults (7 male, mean age 58±11, BMI 24.9±2.4), using incomplete 3x3 Latin square design; 17 randomized, 15 completed all periods, 13-29 days apart. Each subject received all three products once: krill oil (16 capsules, 1400mg EPA+DHA), krill meal (12.3g, 1102mg EPA+DHA), fish oil (10 capsules, 1455mg EPA+DHA), each ~1700mg total omega-3 PUFA, with standardized breakfast. Blood sampled over 72h; primary endpoint was 72h incremental AUC (iAUC) of EPA+DHA in plasma phospholipids.
25884846.findings: Primary endpoint: iAUC of EPA+DHA in plasma phospholipids was significantly higher after krill oil (89.08±33.36 %×h) than krill meal (44.97±18.07, p<0.001) or fish oil (59.15±22.22, p=0.003). Krill meal vs fish oil showed no significant difference (p=0.036, above Bonferroni threshold of 0.017); dose-corrected values were identical. Secondary endpoint iAUC in triglycerides showed no significant differences among products (krill oil 24.46±17.60, fish oil 35.02±26.54, krill meal 25.05±21.18; all p>0.017). High inter-individual variability was observed (iAUC-PL ranges: krill oil 3.45-144.92, fish oil 6.68-94.98, krill meal 4.09-76.57 %×h). No serious adverse events; mild GI symptoms reported with krill products.
25884846.limitations: Small sample (n=15), single-dose acute design measuring short-term phospholipid/triglyceride incorporation rather than long-term tissue status (e.g., erythrocyte Omega-3 Index), as authors note is needed for confirmation. Open-label/single-blind, non-concealed allocation. Capsule numbers/fat amounts differed slightly between products (16 vs 10 capsules; 8g vs 5g fat), a stated limitation. Funded by Olympic Seafood (manufacturer of krill products); one author employed by sponsor; sponsor had no role in data analysis per disclosure.

24098072.background: Krill oil is rich in n-3 PUFAs (EPA/DHA) bound as phosphatidylcholine, unlike fish oils where they are stored as triglycerides. Few studies use objective psychophysiological methods (NIRS, EEG/ERP) to assess n-3 PUFA effects on brain function in elderly people, and it was unclear whether phospholipid vs triglyceride form affects cognitive benefits differently.
24098072.design: RCT, double-blind, parallel-group, 45 healthy Japanese males aged 61-72 (mean 67.1y), randomized to 3 arms (n=15/arm): medium-chain triglycerides (MCT, placebo), krill oil (KO), or sardine oil (SO), 2g/day (8 capsules of 0.25g oil) for 12 weeks. Outcomes: oxyhemoglobin (oxy-Hb) changes via near-infrared spectroscopy and P300 ERP during working memory (2-back) and calculation tasks, measured at weeks 0, 6, 12. 3 dropouts (2 epigastric pain, 1 dermatitis, unrelated to treatment); final n=15 MCT, 13 KO, 14 SO. Funded by Nippon Suisan Kaisha Ltd (krill oil manufacturer); 4 authors were company employees.
24098072.findings: Working memory task: at week 12, oxy-Hb increases at channel 10 were greater in KO (P=0.004) and SO (P=0.043) vs MCT. P300 latency differential at week 12 was significantly lower (faster) in KO vs MCT (Cz P=0.027, Pz P=0.030); no significant P300 amplitude differences at any timepoint. Calculation task: KO showed significantly greater oxy-Hb increase vs MCT at week 12 (channel 15, P=0.006); SO showed no significant effect here. Plasma EPA rose significantly in SO vs MCT at week 12 (P=0.045); no significant EPA difference between KO and MCT despite cognitive effects. No group differences in body weight, BMI, blood pressure, blood/urine tests, or dietary intake.
24098072.limitations: Authors note small sample size (n=13-15/arm) and male-only cohort as major limitations, calling for larger, mixed-sex confirmatory studies. This was a preliminary/pilot-scale trial with multiple comparisons across brain channels/timepoints raising multiplicity concerns; effect on plasma EPA was not significant for KO despite claimed brain benefits, an unexplained inconsistency. Study fully funded by Nippon Suisan Kaisha Ltd (krill oil producer); 4 of 6 authors were company employees, a notable conflict of interest.

31937352.background: Knee osteoarthritis (OA) causes major pain/disability with no approved disease-modifying drugs. Localised joint inflammation (effusion-synovitis) and systemic inflammation contribute to OA pathogenesis, pain and structural progression. Krill oil, rich in EPA/DHA plus astaxanthin with better bioavailability than fish oil, reduced inflammation and pain in small short trials, but prior studies were brief (30 days), lacked imaging outcomes, and did not target patients with inflammatory phenotype (effusion-synovitis). This protocol describes a trial designed to address these gaps.
31937352.design: Multicentre (Hobart, Melbourne, Sydney, Adelaide, Perth), randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled superiority trial (KARAOKE), ACTRN12616000726459. Planned n=260 adults ≥40y with clinical knee OA, VAS pain ≥40mm, and MRI effusion-synovitis grade ≥1; 130 per arm. Intervention: 2×1g softgels/day krill oil (Superba Boost; 190mg/g EPA, 100mg/g DHA) vs identical placebo (vegetable oil blend), for 24 weeks. Randomisation via central website with minimisation, stratified by site; patients, assessors and outcome raters blinded. Primary outcomes: change in knee pain (100mm VAS) and change in MRI effusion-synovitis size over 24 weeks. Intention-to-treat primary analysis using linear mixed models; per-protocol/imputation as secondary. Recruitment completed July 2019; this is a protocol paper without outcome results.
31937352.findings: This is a study protocol; no efficacy results are reported. Sample size calculation: 234 participants (260 with 10% attrition) gives 90% power to detect a 10mm VAS pain difference (based on placebo change of −15.5±25.5mm over 12 weeks in a prior trial) and 90% power to detect a 4.5mL difference in effusion-synovitis volume (baseline ~13.6–13.7mL, SD 8.1–10.7). Cited prior small RCTs found krill oil (300mg or 2g/day) reduced some knee pain/function/stiffness measures and CRP over 30 days versus placebo, motivating this larger, longer, imaging-inclusive trial; actual KARAOKE trial outcomes are not yet available in this paper.
31937352.limitations: Protocol only—no efficacy/safety results reported yet; findings pending. Convenience sampling rather than population-based recruitment. No data safety monitoring board used (justified by krill oil's presumed good safety profile). Funded by NHMRC and University of Tasmania (no role in design/analysis), plus industry funding and in-kind product supply from Aker Biomarine (krill oil/placebo manufacturer), a potential conflict of interest; authors declare no competing interests. Subgroup and per-protocol analyses planned but exploratory. Single-blind ultrasound sub-study only in Perth; reproducibility of ultrasound noted as operator-dependent.

26504524.background: Type 2 diabetes carries high cardiovascular disease risk, including endothelial dysfunction, dyslipidemia, and insulin resistance. Krill oil is a phospholipid-bound ω-3 fatty acid source (EPA/DHA) with astaxanthin, proposed to have better bioavailability than fish oil. This trial tested whether krill oil supplementation improves endothelial function, lipids, glucose control, and insulin resistance in type 2 diabetes patients, meeting AHA's 1000mg/day ω-3 recommendation.
26504524.design: Randomized, double-blind, cross-over trial in 47-48 adults with type 2 diabetes (mean age 64.8y, 66% male) at Danbury Hospital, CT. Participants received 2 capsules/day krill oil (1000mg ω-3 total) or olive oil for 4 weeks, 2-week washout, then crossed over for 4 weeks. Endpoints (EndoPAT RHI, lipids, glucose, HbA1c, C peptide, HOMA2-IR, antioxidant capacity) measured at baseline, T1, T2. 34 of 47 participants then completed an optional, non-randomized open-label 17-week krill oil extension compared to baseline. Funded by Prograde Inc (also supplied both oils).
26504524.findings: Primary endpoint: 4-week krill oil vs olive oil significantly improved endothelial function (RHI 2.04±0.52 vs 1.83±0.56, p=0.025), reduced C peptide (0.822±0.39 vs 0.933±0.47 ng/mL, p=0.029; significant only in non-insulin users, p=0.034), and lowered HOMA-IR (2.30±0.91 vs 2.64±1.23, p=0.019). No significant differences in HbA1c, TC (p=0.078, near-significant), HDL, LDL, triglycerides, glucose, or antioxidant capacity. After 17-week krill oil extension vs baseline (n=34): RHI improved (2.16±0.73 vs 1.90±0.54, p=0.041) and HDL increased (49.09±15.63 vs 43.48±14.10 mg/dL, p=0.002); but C peptide and HOMA-IR reductions were no longer significant (p=0.599, p=0.874), and HbA1c/glucose remained unchanged.
26504524.limitations: Small sample (47, dropping to 34 for extension); extension phase was open-label, uncontrolled, non-randomized comparison to baseline only. Olive oil comparator contained trace ALA (8mg/day), a potential mild confounder. No blood pressure measurements despite high hypertension prevalence (72-74%). Free-living design allowed uncontrolled diet/activity. Single-site study; funded and supplement-supplied by manufacturer Prograde Inc, though authors declared no competing interests. Authors call for larger, longer trials and dose-comparison studies.

42144109.background: EPA/DHA supplementation benefits are inconsistent across trials, possibly due to sex, APOE4 genotype, and chemical form of ω-3 (phospholipid in krill oil vs triglyceride in fish oil). This trial compared matched EPA+DHA doses from krill vs fish oil on plasma ω-3 levels, and tested effect modification by sex and APOE4 status, to inform strategies for optimizing ω-3 status, relevant to late-onset Alzheimer's prevention.
42144109.design: Double-blind RCT (NCT04279743) in 72 healthy adults (53F/19M, aged 30-65y) matched for age/BMI, stratified by sex and APOE genotype. Krill oil (n=36: 706mg EPA+393mg DHA/d) vs fish oil (n=36: 738mg EPA+462mg DHA/d), ~1.1g/d total ω-3, 4 capsules/d for 12 weeks. Plasma fatty acids measured by GC-FID at baseline, weeks 1,2,4,12. Randomization computer-generated; staff blinded to allocation and genotype. Primary outcome: change from baseline in EPA/DHA (2-way ANOVA treatment×time); secondary: 3-way ANOVA with sex/APOE4.
42144109.findings: Significant time×treatment interaction for ΔEPA (P=0.0001) and ΔDHA (P=0.005): krill oil gave ~1.5-fold higher increases than fish oil. At 12wk, ΔEPA=6.88±0.39 mg/dL (krill) vs 4.90±0.40 (fish); ΔDHA=4.22±0.31 (krill) vs 2.84±0.34 (fish), i.e., 1.4-fold and 1.5-fold higher with krill. Time×sex interaction significant for EPA only (P=0.026): females had ~1.5-fold greater ΔEPA increase than males; DHA response not sex-dependent. APOE4 carriers showed 3-fold EPA and 1.6-fold DHA increases vs baseline (P<0.001), but not significantly different from noncarriers (null genotype interaction). No adverse effects reported; compliance ~96-97%, not different between groups.
42144109.limitations: Sample size (n=72) fell short of original target (n=160), limiting power for secondary/3-way interactions (sex×treatment×APOE4), making those analyses exploratory. Sex distribution imbalanced (more females) and APOE4 carriers skewed toward females, further limiting genotype analysis. Only plasma (not erythrocyte) fatty acids reported here; undiagnosed prodromal cognitive impairment not excluded. Single-center, healthy middle-aged adults only, limiting generalizability. Funded by Canadian Institutes of Health Research; authors report no conflicts of interest; funder had no role in design/analysis.

34989797.background: Severe hypertriglyceridemia (TG ≥500 mg/dL) affects ~2% of US adults and raises pancreatitis/ASCVD risk. Novel ω-3 formulations with higher bioavailability are of interest. ω-3–PL/FFA (CaPre) is a krill oil-derived agent with EPA/DHA as ~50:50 free fatty acids and phospholipid esters, previously shown in phase 2 to lower TG without raising LDL-C. TRILOGY tested phase 3 efficacy/safety in severe hypertriglyceridemia.
34989797.design: Pooled analysis of TRILOGY 1 (n=242, US) and TRILOGY 2 (n=278, US/Canada/Mexico), identical double-blind, placebo-controlled RCTs. 520 adults with fasting TG 500-1500 mg/dL randomized 2.5:1 to ω-3–PL/FFA 4 g/d (1.24 g/d EPA+DHA) or cornstarch placebo for 26 weeks. Primary endpoint: % change in TG at 12 weeks (ITT, ANCOVA, multiple imputation); key secondary at 26 weeks. Neither individual trial reached significance alone due to unexpectedly large placebo TG drops; pooling was prespecified after both trials completed.
34989797.findings: Primary endpoint met: TG fell 26.0% (95% CI 20.5-31.5) with ω-3–PL/FFA vs 15.1% (6.6-23.5) placebo at 12 weeks (difference -10.9%, 95% CI -20.4 to -1.5; P=.02), persisting at 26 weeks (-33.5% vs -20.8%; difference -12.7%, P=.02). No significant treatment differences for non-HDL-C, VLDL-C, HDL-C, or LDL-C at 12 weeks (all P≥.18); non-HDL-C reached significance at 26 weeks (-5.8%, P=.04) but VLDL-C, HDL-C, LDL-C remained null. LDL-C and ApoB were not significantly increased. More patients achieved TG<500mg/dL with active treatment (56.5% vs 45.9% at 12wk; NNT~11). Effects tended larger in statin/CAI users and those with lower baseline EPA+DHA (interaction P=.08, exploratory). Adverse events, serious AEs, and discontinuations were similar between groups; no deaths; one atrial fibrillation event in active arm.
34989797.limitations: Authors note large, likely regression-to-mean-driven placebo TG reduction weakened per-trial power, necessitating pooling (post hoc, unadjusted for multiplicity—results labeled exploratory). Nonparametric sensitivity analysis attenuated significance at 26 weeks (median difference P=.11). Subgroup findings (statin users, low baseline EPA+DHA) are hypothesis-generating only. Industry-funded (Acasti Pharma), with sponsor involvement in design/interpretation; several authors are company employees/stockholders or paid consultants/investigators; independent statistician performed analyses. Double-blind, randomized, large (n=520), 26-week duration—solid design overall.

39974718.background: Fish oil (FO) and krill oil (KO) are both major sources of Omega-3 PUFAs but differ in molecular form (triglyceride/ethyl ester vs phospholipid), which may affect bioavailability. No comprehensive comparison across formulations and doses existed, leaving unclear guidance on which source/dose best optimizes absorption for clinical and nutritional use.
39974718.design: Network meta-analysis (PRISMA-NMA, PROSPERO CRD42024532536) of 26 RCTs/multi-arm trials (2003–2023) from 5 databases. Outcomes: Omega-3 index (O3i, 22 studies), AUC (5), Tmax (4), Cmax (5), across FO and KO molecular forms/doses (low <2000mg, medium 2000-2900mg, high >3000mg DHA+EPA/day). Comparators: vegetable oils/placebo. Random-effects netmeta in R; PEDro risk-of-bias; SUCRA rankings; Egger's test for bias. No blinding/randomization details of primary trials pooled beyond PEDro scoring (9 excellent, 15 good, 2 moderate quality).
39974718.findings: O3i: most FO forms beat placebo (e.g., FO-rTAG<2: MD 4.04, p<0.0001); FO-EE>3000mg was non-significant (MD 1.9, p=0.12); KO<2000mg significantly raised O3i (MD 1.64, p<0.0001) but KO-HPL/KO-LPL did not (p=0.25, p=0.88). AUC: KO-PL/FFA<2000mg beat FO-rTAG (MD -14.26, p=0.0085) and FO-EE (MD -18.63, p=0.0008). Tmax: FO-EE>3000mg trend toward faster Tmax vs KO-PL/FFA (MD -8.47, p=0.054, borderline). Cmax: FO emulsions (EMN, EMS) significantly exceeded FO capsules (p=0.0007, p=0.0002); KO-PL/FFA differences vs FO forms were non-significant (p>0.05). High heterogeneity noted for O3i (I2=97.1%) and Tmax (I2=94.8%); AUC/Cmax subgroups showed low-to-high heterogeneity. No publication bias detected (Egger's p>0.05).
39974718.limitations: Authors note high heterogeneity (especially Tmax, Cmax), limited studies, and narrower KO dose range (<1900mg) vs FO (up to >3000mg), preventing direct high-dose comparisons. Several key findings (Tmax, some O3i/Cmax comparisons) were statistically non-significant despite trends. This is a network meta-analysis of published trials, not new primary data; underlying trial blinding/randomization varied and wasn't detailed per study. Funded by China Medical University; authors declare no competing interests.

24304605.background: Krill oil (phospholipid-bound n-3 PUFA) has been hypothesized to have higher bioavailability than fish oil (triglyceride-bound n-3 PUFA), potentially improving omega-3 index and CVD risk markers more effectively. Prior trials showed only non-significant trends favoring krill oil. This study aimed to directly compare krill oil vs fish oil vs placebo on plasma/RBC fatty acid profiles and lipids in healthy adults using a longer-term randomized crossover design.
24304605.design: Double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled crossover trial in 24 healthy adults (12M/12F, mean age 28y). Three 4-week phases (krill oil, fish oil, corn oil placebo), each providing 600 mg/d n-3 PUFA (6×500mg capsules/d), separated by 8-week washouts. Krill oil (K•REAL) and fish oil (Omevital TG 18/12) matched for n-3 PUFA dose. Endpoints: plasma/RBC fatty acids, serum lipids, safety/tolerability. Stratified randomization by sex to treatment sequence; ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01323036.
24304605.findings: Krill oil raised RBC omega-3 index more than fish oil (change 1.04% vs 0.47%; p=0.0043) and vs control (p<0.0001). Krill oil increased plasma EPA+DHA more than fish oil (p=0.0011) and reduced n-6:n-3 ratio vs fish oil (plasma p=0.0043, RBC p=0.0143). Both oils raised plasma/RBC EPA, DHA, total n-3 PUFA vs control (p<0.0001–0.014). Total and LDL cholesterol rose similarly with krill (TC p=0.0067, LDL p=0.0143) and fish oil (TC p=0.0028, LDL p=0.0143) vs control; HDL and triglycerides unchanged across all arms (null). No differences between krill and fish oil in TC, LDL, or TC/HDL. No adverse events; compliance ~96-97%; krill oil caused more burping/aftertaste than fish oil/control.
24304605.limitations: Small sample (n=24), short 4-week intervention phases (may not reach steady-state), free-living design without strict dietary/macronutrient control, uncontrolled n-6 PUFA intake and differing n-6 content between oils (krill 1.73g/100g vs fish 21.95g/100g) could confound n-6:n-3 ratio results. Funded/study designed by Enzymotec Ltd (krill oil manufacturer); two authors (IE, SZ) are Enzymotec employees; other authors declare no conflicts. Randomized double-blind crossover design is a methodological strength but generalizability limited to healthy normolipidemic adults.

26537218.background: Krill oil's EPA/DHA are bound mostly to phospholipids (PL) rather than triglycerides, which may enhance bioavailability. This study tested whether the amount of PL in krill oil (high vs low), at equal n-3 PUFA dose, affects the rate of incorporation of EPA/DHA into plasma and red blood cells (RBC), a marker linked to CVD risk reduction.
26537218.design: 20 healthy adults (of 24 enrolled) completed a semi-randomized, single-blind crossover trial: 1.5 g/day low-PL krill oil (LPL, 3 capsules), 3 g/day high-PL krill oil (HPL, 6 capsules), or 3 g/day corn oil placebo (6 capsules), each 4 weeks, separated by 8-week washouts. Both krill oils delivered 600 mg/day total n-3 PUFA (600 vs 1200 mg/day PL). LPL phase was added last, non-randomized, reducing blinding integrity; earlier 3 phases were double-blind, randomized (NCT01323036).
26537218.findings: Plasma EPA, DPA, DHA, n-3 PUFA and EPA+DHA rose similarly with LPL and HPL vs control (all p<0.001), with no significant difference between krill oils. In RBC, both oils increased EPA vs control (p<0.001) and reduced n-6 PUFA (LPL p<0.001, HPL p=0.007), but HPL increased RBC EPA, DPA, total/n-3 PUFA more than LPL (p<0.001). LPL did not significantly change RBC EPA+DHA (omega-3 index) or n-6:n-3 ratio vs control, whereas HPL increased EPA+DHA and decreased n-6:n-3 ratio vs both control and LPL (p<0.001). HPL raised total and LDL cholesterol vs control (p<0.005); LPL did not alter these lipids. No adverse events attributable to treatment; compliance 94.6–97.4%.
26537218.limitations: Small sample (n=20 completers), single-blind and only semi-randomized (LPL phase added last, non-randomized, unequal capsule numbers between arms compromising blinding). Authors note this affects double-blinding. Healthy normolipidemic population limits generalizability to at-risk groups. Funded/authored with Enzymotec Ltd (krill oil manufacturer) employees among co-authors (IE, SZ, IS); VRR and PJHJ declare no conflicts.

29372051.background: Marine n-3 fatty acids from fish/fish oil may reduce CVD risk, mainly via TAG lowering, but evidence is inconsistent. Krill oil is an alternative n-3 source with EPA/DHA largely bound to phospholipids rather than TAG, but few human studies have tested its cardiovascular effects, including on detailed lipoprotein subclasses.
29372051.design: 8-week randomised, controlled, parallel trial (Norway) in 36 healthy adults (18-70y, fasting TAG 1.3-4.0 mmol/l) completing intervention (n=12/arm). Fish group: 3 weekly fish meals (cod, salmon, mackerel) per dietary guidelines. Krill group: 8 capsules/d (4 g/d krill oil, RIMFROST Sublime). Control group: 8 capsules/d (4 g/d high-oleic sunflower oil). Weekly marine n-3 intake: 4103 mg (fish), 4654 mg (krill), 0 mg (control). Randomised 1:1:1, stratified by sex/age, block randomisation by external statistician; krill/control double-blinded (successful blinding, ~5/12 correctly guessed each). Primary outcome: fasting serum TAG. Study underpowered (needed 96, achieved 40 randomised due to recruitment difficulty).
29372051.findings: Primary endpoint null: fasting TAG fell 17% (krill, -0.29 mmol/l), 7% (fish, -0.10), 1% (control, -0.02) with no significant within- or between-group differences (P=0.59). Krill oil significantly increased total lipids (P=0.007), phospholipids (P=0.015), cholesterol (P=0.009), cholesteryl esters (P=0.022) and non-esterified cholesterol (P=0.002) in smallest VLDL subclass vs other groups; HDL3-cholesterol and LDL-TAG rose in krill and fish groups (P=0.009, P=0.002). Fasting glucose fell 5.6→5.3 mmol/l in krill vs rise in others (krill vs control P=0.01). Vitamin D rose 56→72 nmol/l in fish group vs fall in krill (P=0.004). Plasma EPA, DPA, DHA rose significantly in fish/krill vs control (all P≤0.0003). No changes in total/LDL/HDL cholesterol, blood pressure, or physical tests; none of the biochemical/clinical changes survived multiple-comparison correction.
29372051.limitations: Study markedly underpowered for primary TAG outcome (40 of planned 96 randomised) due to recruitment difficulty; not a fully controlled dietary intervention (habitual diet/activity self-maintained); control oil (high-oleic sunflower) not a true inert placebo, though no plasma fatty acid changes seen in that arm. Lipoprotein subclass analysis was exploratory/unadjusted for multiple comparisons. Small sample (n=12/arm), single-center, 8 weeks. Funded partly by Rimfrost AS (krill oil manufacturer); co-author employed by Rimfrost (no stock); other authors disclosed unrelated industry funding/honoraria.

21862301.background: Chemical form (TAG, ethyl-ester [EE], phospholipid [PL]) may affect omega-3 FA bioavailability. Krill oil EPA+DHA is largely PL-bound, and prior claims suggested superior bioavailability, but no study had compared identical doses of krill oil PL vs fish oil re-esterified TAG (rTAG) and EE directly. This crossover trial tested that comparison using plasma phospholipid FA incorporation as a proxy for bioavailability.
21862301.design: Double-blinded, randomized 3-way crossover in 12 healthy men (mean age 31y, BMI 24.6), each receiving single doses of rTAG, EE, and krill oil (14-day washout between), 1680 mg EPA+DHA/day (rTAG/EE: 1008mg EPA+672mg DHA; krill oil: 1050mg EPA+630mg DHA). Blood drawn pre-dose and at 2,4,6,8,24,48,72h; plasma phospholipid FA composition was primary endpoint, analyzed via GC. AUC0-72h, cmax, tmax compared by ANOVA with Bonferroni post-hoc.
21862301.findings: Krill oil produced highest EPA+DHA incorporation into plasma PL (AUC0-72h 80.03±34.71%*h) vs rTAG (59.78±36.75) and EE (47.53±38.42), but differences were not statistically significant (p=0.119) due to high variability. EPA AUC showed a trend (p=0.057), with rTAG vs krill oil trend p=0.086. cmax for EPA+DHA differed significantly overall (p=0.039), driven by krill oil vs EE (p=0.034). DHA, total n-3 FA AUC and tmax showed no significant differences. Krill oil unexpectedly contained 22% of EPA and 21% of DHA as free fatty acids; fish oil samples had none.
21862301.limitations: Single-dose, crossover pharmacokinetic study (not chronic), small sample (n=12, healthy young men only), yielding high SD and mostly nonsignificant results—authors explicitly call findings preliminary, needing larger/longer trials. Plasma phospholipid FA is not necessarily representative of tissue status. Krill oil dosing required slightly more total fat intake, a potential confound. No safety/tolerability data. Fish oil supplements donated by manufacturer (Dr. Loges); two authors serve as industry consultants; von Schacky has industry ties and founded the analysis lab used.

26557185.background: This is a correspondence/response article clarifying a prior study (Skarpańska-Stejnborn et al., 2010) that examined whether krill oil supplementation, given its purported antioxidant properties, could attenuate oxidative stress and inflammatory markers induced by exhaustive exercise in athletes (rowers). It also corrects a product-naming error (mislabeling "Krill Oil" as "Neptune Krill Oil") and discloses supplement composition and funding details omitted from the original paper.
26557185.design: Original study population: rowers, divided into a supplemented group and a placebo group, both undergoing the same training loads and exhaustive exercise tests. Supplement: Krill Oil (Enzymotec Ltd, India), composition per 100g included 42g phospholipids, 28g DHA+EPA (17g EPA, 11g DHA), 31g Omega-3, 0.19g astaxanthin, 142 IU/g vitamin A. Exact dose administered to athletes and duration are not specified in this text; n per arm, randomization and blinding details are not stated in this correspondence.
26557185.findings: The response reaffirms the original findings: krill oil supplementation was associated with a significant reduction in oxidative stress in rowers, evidenced by decreased post-exercise erythrocyte lipid peroxidation damage in the supplemented group, with no such beneficial effect observed in the placebo group. No specific numerical values (means, percentages, p-values) are provided in this text. Since training loads and exercise tests were identical between groups, the authors attribute the difference to supplementation.
26557185.limitations: This is a letter/response to a critique, not a full primary study report, so detailed methodology, sample size, randomization, and blinding are not described here. Funding was solely from statutory university funds, not previously disclosed in the original paper; no external grant or conflict of interest information is given. No p-values or effect sizes are reported in this text, limiting quantitative assessment of the reaffirmed findings.

29222893.background: Krill oil (KO) and fish oil (FO) both supply EPA/DHA, but studies on comparative bioavailability are inconsistent, often mixing genders/ages and reporting high variability. Gender affects LC n-3 PUFA metabolism. This study aimed to compare postprandial plasma EPA/DHA/DPA response to KO vs FO vs olive oil (OO) control in a narrow-age female cohort, to reduce inter-individual variability seen in prior mixed-sex studies.
29222893.design: Randomised, controlled, single-dose, three-way crossover study in 10 healthy women (18-45y, BMI 20-30). Each participant received, in random order with ≥7-day washout, a high-fat breakfast (150g mashed potato+15g olive oil) plus either 5x1g KO capsules (907mg total LC n-3 PUFA, 542mg EPA), 5x1g FO capsules (1441mg LC n-3 PUFA, 786mg EPA), or 5g olive oil control. Capsules (not liquid oils) used for partial blinding, but colour differed so blinding was incomplete. Blood drawn fasting and hourly for 5h. Power calculated for n=6; n=10 completed. Sponsor/funding not stated beyond oils purchased commercially (Swisse); authors declared no conflicts.
29222893.findings: Plasma EPA rose significantly from 2h after both KO and FO vs OO (p<0.05), plateauing by ~3h; no significant difference between KO and FO net iAUC for EPA (p=0.850) despite FO's iAUC being 12% higher, or for total EPA+DPA+DHA (p=0.980). DHA and DPA showed no consistent significant increases across groups (mostly null, sporadic single-timepoint differences, e.g., DHA KO vs FO at 2h p=0.040). No significant treatment effects on plasma or chylomicron cholesterol, TAG, LDL, HDL, or glucose (only time effects significant); chylomicron TAG rose with FO at 1-2h (p<0.05) but normalized by 4h. Pilot lipid-fraction data (n=4) suggested EPA from KO localized more to plasma phospholipids vs TAG for FO, without formal significance testing.
29222893.limitations: Authors note: very small sample (n=10, subgroup analyses n=4), short observation window (5h, insufficient given reported EPA/DHA Tmax of 10-55h in other studies), incomplete blinding (capsule colour differed), unequal LC n-3 PUFA doses between KO (907mg) and FO (1441mg, 37% higher) by design, and single-gender (women only) limiting generalisability to men. High inter-participant variability likely limited power to detect KO-FO differences. No faecal loss measured, so "bioavailability" terminology is imprecise per authors. Crossover RCT design, single-dose, no external funding disclosed, no conflicts declared.

41933837.background: Chronic musculoskeletal (MSK) pain is common and disabling in older adults, whose pharmacologic options carry risks. Omega-3 LC-PUFAs (EPA/DHA) have anti-inflammatory/analgesic properties, but intake and blood levels are low in older US adults. Krill oil offers phospholipid-bound EPA/DHA plus astaxanthin and choline, potentially aiding pain, but feasibility/efficacy data in older adults with chronic MSK pain were lacking. This pilot aimed to test feasibility/acceptability and explore preliminary pain effects.
41933837.design: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled 12-week pilot trial (KOPE) in 40 community-dwelling adults ≥60y with moderate chronic hip/knee/low-back pain (≥4/10), stratified by sex, 1:1 to krill oil (n=20; 4 g/d, 1288 mg/d EPA+DHA, 0.45 mg astaxanthin, 320 mg choline) or matched placebo (n=20; mixed vegetable oil, no EPA/DHA). Visits at weeks 0, 6, 12. Primary outcomes: feasibility (recruitment, retention, adherence, acceptability); secondary: omega-3/inflammatory biomarkers; exploratory: pain intensity/interference, WOMAC, pain sites, PGIC, physical function. Intention-to-treat, mixed-effects models adjusted for age, sex, BMI.
41933837.findings: Recruitment met in 8 months; retention 95% (38/40); adherence >70% threshold met by 100% (self-report) or 83.3% (capsule count) of krill oil group vs 89.5%/83.3% placebo; acceptability 7.7±2.3/10, no group differences (P>0.17). No serious adverse events; GI symptoms most common, more related AEs in placebo (5 vs 2). Omega-3 index rose from 4.3% to 7.4% with krill oil vs no change in placebo (Δ=3.0%, 95% CI 1.9–4.0, d=4.40); no CRP change. Exploratory pain results favored krill oil: pain intensity ΔKO−ΔP=−1.05 (95% CI −2.72,0.62, d=−0.77, not significant); pain sites rate ratio 0.59 (95% CI 0.41–0.84); PGIC improvement 66.7% vs 40.0% (aOR 4.35, 95% CI 0.97–19.55). WOMAC and PEG changes were small/non-significant. No meaningful between-group differences in physical function (SPPB, grip strength, 6-min walk, PAT-D).
41933837.limitations: Authors state this pilot (n=40, single academic center, mostly non-Hispanic White) was not powered for efficacy/safety conclusions; short 12-week duration may be insufficient for functional outcomes; findings are preliminary and require a fully powered RCT. No conflicts of interest reported; funded by NIA/NIH grants; krill oil and placebo supplied free by Aker BioMarine (sponsor had no role in design/analysis). Wide, often non-significant confidence intervals for pain outcomes (e.g., pain intensity, PGIC) indicate uncertainty.

21042875.background: Fish is a limited resource, spurring interest in Antarctic krill oil as an alternative marine n-3 PUFA source. Krill oil's EPA/DHA is mainly bound to phospholipids rather than triglycerides (as in fish oil), raising questions about relative bioavailability and effects on lipids, oxidative stress, and inflammation. This study compared krill oil and fish oil supplementation on plasma n-3 fatty acid levels, serum lipids, and inflammatory/oxidative markers in healthy volunteers.
21042875.design: Open-label, single-center, randomized, parallel-group trial in 113-122 healthy volunteers (normal/slightly elevated cholesterol/TG) analyzed per protocol. Groups: krill oil 3.0 g/day (6 capsules, EPA+DHA=543 mg, N=36 analyzed), fish oil 1.8 g/day (3 capsules, EPA+DHA=864 mg, N=40), and no-supplement control (N=37), for 7 weeks. Not blinded (open design); randomization used but blinding/allocation concealment not described. Funded partly by Aker BioMarine ASA (krill oil manufacturer); two authors employed by Aker BioMarine.
21042875.findings: Plasma EPA, DHA, and DPA rose significantly in both krill oil and fish oil groups vs control (e.g., EPA +44.5 vs +45.2 µmol/L, DHA +19.4 vs +23.4 µmol/L; both p<0.0001 vs control), with no significant difference between krill and fish oil despite krill's EPA+DHA dose being only 62.8% of fish oil's. Arachidonic acid increased in krill group but decreased in fish oil group (between-group p=0.001). No significant between-group differences in HDL, LDL, triglycerides, total cholesterol, ApoA1, ApoB100, HDL/TG ratio, hsCRP, inflammation/hemostasis markers, α-tocopherol, or urinary F2-isoprostanes (oxidative stress). Only within-group LDL rise in fish oil group reached significance (p=0.039); within-group HDL/TG ratio rise in krill group was significant (p=0.016), but not between groups. No safety concerns; adverse events similar across groups.
21042875.limitations: Open-label (not blinded), single-center design with no placebo capsule for supplement groups; author-noted per-protocol exclusions (2 krill subjects) and unequal EPA/DHA doses complicate direct comparison. Sample size modest (~36-40/arm), short 7-week duration, healthy population limits generalizability to those with dyslipidemia/metabolic syndrome (as authors suggest for future study). Partial industry funding by krill oil manufacturer (Aker BioMarine) and co-authors employed there represent a conflict of interest.

28371906.background: Krill oil, rich in phospholipid-bound EPA/DHA and antioxidants (astaxanthin, vitamin E), has been proposed as a lipid-modifying agent, but evidence across trials was inconclusive. This systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs was conducted to clarify krill oil's effects on plasma lipid parameters (total cholesterol, LDL-C, HDL-C, triglycerides).
28371906.design: Systematic review/meta-analysis (PubMed, Scopus to March 25, 2016) of 7 RCTs (14 treatment arms; 662 participants: 427 krill oil, 235 control), from Canada, Norway, USA. Krill oil doses ranged 500mg/d to 4g/d (500mg capsules/softgels), duration 4 weeks to 3 months. 4 parallel-group, 3 crossover trials; most double-blind, placebo-controlled. Populations included healthy volunteers and dyslipidemic/type 2 diabetic adults. Random/fixed-effects models used per heterogeneity; WMD with 95%CI as effect size.
28371906.findings: Krill oil significantly reduced LDL-C (WMD -15.52 mg/dL; 95%CI -28.43 to -2.61; P=0.018) and triglycerides (WMD -14.03 mg/dL; 95%CI -21.38 to -6.67; P<0.001), and significantly increased HDL-C (WMD +6.65 mg/dL; 95%CI 2.30–10.99; P=0.003). Total cholesterol reduction was not significant (WMD -7.50 mg/dL; 95%CI -17.94 to 2.93; P=0.159). Effects on TC, LDL-C, TG were significant only in trials ≥12 weeks; HDL-C rise was significant in both shorter and longer trials. LDL-C and HDL-C effects were driven largely by one study (Bunea et al. 2004); removing it left only TG-lowering significant. No adverse events attributable to krill oil; mild GI symptoms only.
28371906.limitations: Small number of studies (7) with small sample sizes and heterogeneous populations; publication bias suggested by funnel plot/Begg's/Egger's tests for TC, LDL-C, HDL-C (trim-and-fill adjusted TG estimate: -15.12 mg/dL). LDL-C/HDL-C findings not robust to sensitivity analysis (driven by one trial). Sequence generation/allocation concealment risk unclear in most studies. Krill oil composition may vary by species/season; dietary background not well controlled. No external funding; authors declared no conflicts of interest.

26328782.background: Fish (fish oil EE/TG) and krill oil are both marketed sources of EPA+DHA, but prior bioavailability comparisons were confounded by mismatched doses, capsule counts, and EPA/DHA amounts, fueling claims that krill's phospholipid form is better absorbed. This trial matched dose and EPA/DHA content across products to test true relative bioavailability over a longer (4-week) supplementation period, since prior conflicting studies used single-dose or unequal-dose designs.
26328782.design: Randomized, double-blind, three-arm, parallel, multi-dose trial (NCT02427373) in 66 healthy adults (n=22/arm, mean age 35, 73% female). Arms: fish oil-EE, fish oil-TG, or krill oil, each providing 1.3 g/d EPA+DHA (~816 mg EPA + 522 mg DHA/d), 6 capsules/day for 28 days. Plasma/RBC fatty acids sampled at baseline, 4,8,12,48,72,336,672h. Primary endpoint: total plasma EPA+DHA at 672h (Week 4), analyzed by ANCOVA (intent-to-treat), with pairwise bioequivalence (two one-sided t-tests, GMR/90%CI).
26328782.findings: Primary endpoint: plasma EPA+DHA at Week 4 was not significantly different between groups (fish oil-EE 90.9±41; fish oil-TG 108±40; krill oil 118.5±48 µg/mL; p=0.052), differing by <24%. RBC EPA+DHA also similar (39.6±13, 44.5±12, 46.1±13 µg/mL; p=0.19), differing <14%. EPA alone in plasma: p=0.17 (no sig. difference). DHA alone in plasma: p=0.013 (significant), with fish oil-EE somewhat lower at 336–672h; fish oil-TG vs krill trend toward bioequivalence (GMR=0.95, 0.79–1.13, p=0.059). No serious AEs; 11 AEs in 9 subjects, mostly mild GI/nausea/headache, not differing by group.
26328782.limitations: Authors note wider variability/confidence intervals in plasma levels, possibly from inter-individual variability and modest parallel-group sample size (n=22/arm); a larger or crossover study could clarify findings. Primary plasma EPA+DHA endpoint narrowly missed significance (p=0.052) and DHA alone differed significantly by formulation, showing not fully null result. Study funded and conducted by DSM Nutritional Products (oil manufacturer); authors are DSM employees; CRO Worldwide Clinical Trials was compensated by DSM—notable conflict of interest.

30261756.background: Metabolites in the choline oxidation and tryptophan degradation pathways have been linked to lifestyle diseases and dietary habits. Krill oil is a source of ω-3 PUFAs that is also rich in phosphatidylcholine, so the study aimed to see how it affects plasma choline-, homocysteine- and vitamin-related metabolites.
30261756.design: Pilot study, 17 healthy volunteers aged 18-36 years, given 4.5 g krill oil per day (providing 833 mg ω-3 PUFAs and 1750 mg phosphatidylcholine) for 28 days. The abstract does not mention a placebo control or blinding, so it appears to be a single-arm, open-label intervention with pre/post measurements.
30261756.findings: Fasting plasma choline increased by 28.4% (p<.001), betaine by 26.6% (p<.001), dimethylglycine by 33.7% (p<.001), and sarcosine by 16.8% (p<.001). No statistically significant changes were seen for glycine, serine, methionine, total homocysteine, cysteine, cystathionine, methionine sulfoxide, folate, cobalamin, B2, B3, and B6 vitamers, tryptophan, kynurenines, nicotinamide, vitamin A, or vitamin E. Overall, krill oil affected choline metabolite levels but not tryptophan-kynurenine-nicotinamide pathway metabolites or vitamin status.
