30261756.limitations: This was a small (n=17), uncontrolled pilot study with no stated placebo group or blinding, and short duration (28 days) in young healthy adults only. The authors themselves note the need for confirmation in a placebo-controlled trial including an ω-3 PUFA-only arm (without phospholipids) to separate the contributions of different active ingredients. No information on long-term or clinical outcomes is provided.

19854375.background: Antarctic krill (Euphausia superba) oil is rich in EPA and DHA, omega-3 fatty acids linked to cardiovascular and metabolic benefits. This study tested whether krill oil could raise plasma EPA/DHA levels similarly to a known fish oil source (menhaden oil), while checking that it was safe and well tolerated, in overweight/obese adults.
19854375.design: Randomized, double-blind, parallel-arm trial in 76 overweight and obese men and women. Participants received 2 g/day of krill oil, menhaden oil, or control (olive) oil capsules for 4 weeks. Outcomes measured included plasma EPA/DHA levels, blood pressure, blood urea nitrogen, and other safety/tolerability parameters.
19854375.findings: Both krill oil and menhaden oil significantly increased plasma EPA and DHA compared with control (P < .001): krill oil raised EPA by 178.4 ± 38.7 µmol/L and DHA by 90.2 ± 40.3 µmol/L; menhaden oil raised EPA by 131.8 ± 28.0 µmol/L and DHA by 149.9 ± 30.4 µmol/L; control changes were minimal (EPA 2.9 ± 13.8, DHA -1.1 ± 32.4 µmol/L). Systolic blood pressure decreased more in the menhaden oil group than control (P < .05), while the krill oil group's blood pressure response did not differ significantly from either group. Blood urea nitrogen declined in the krill oil group compared with menhaden oil (P < .006). No other significant differences in safety variables or adverse events were reported. Overall, krill oil supplementation increased plasma EPA and DHA and appeared well tolerated with no evidence of adverse safety effects.
19854375.limitations: This is a randomized, double-blind, controlled trial, but with a relatively small sample size (N = 76) and short duration (4 weeks), limiting ability to assess long-term effects or rare adverse events. The abstract does not specify how blinding was verified or provide details on dropout rates, exact demographic breakdown, or statistical methods beyond p-values, and no information is given about longer-term metabolic or cardiovascular outcomes.

36566465.background: Antarctic krill oil (KO) is rich in n-3 PUFAs (EPA/DHA), phospholipids (which may boost n-3 PUFA absorption vs fish oil), and astaxanthin, an antioxidant. KO has known anti-inflammatory/immunomodulatory effects, and n-3 PUFAs are purported to aid muscular recovery. This study tested whether KO supplementation could improve muscular performance recovery and reduce oxidative stress, inflammation, and muscle damage markers after resistance exercise.
36566465.design: Randomized controlled trial in 30 college-aged, resistance-trained males (~20.4 years, ~74 kg, ~180 cm). Participants received either 3 g/d krill oil or placebo for 3 days before a muscle-damaging resistance exercise bout, and continued supplementation for 3 days after. Outcomes—knee isokinetic strength, 20 m sprint, hexagon test, and blood markers (CK, LDH, SOD, T-AOC, ROS, MDA, IL-2, IL-6, TNF-α)—were measured before supplementation, and immediately (0 h), 6 h, 24 h, 48 h, and 72 h post-exercise. Placebo-controlled; blinding status not specified in abstract.
36566465.findings: Compared with placebo, the KO group showed: significantly lower serum creatine kinase (CK) at 24 h and 48 h post-exercise; faster (lower) hexagon test times at 6 h and 24 h; greater recovery of isokinetic muscle strength at 24 h and 48 h, with apparent over-recovery at 72 h; significantly higher superoxide dismutase (SOD) at 0, 6, and 24 h; higher total antioxidant capacity (T-AOC) at 0, 6, and 72 h; and lower malondialdehyde (MDA) at 6 h. No significant differences were found between groups in IL-2, IL-6, or TNF-α. Overall, KO supplementation was associated with reduced markers of exercise-induced muscle damage and improved recovery.
36566465.limitations: Small sample size (n=30, all young resistance-trained males), limiting generalizability to other populations (e.g., women, older adults, untrained individuals). The abstract does not specify blinding (single/double-blind) or randomization method details beyond "randomly supplemented." Short supplementation duration (3 days before, 3 days after) may not reflect longer-term effects. No inflammatory marker differences were observed despite proposed anti-inflammatory mechanism, suggesting effects may be more antioxidant/muscle-damage-related than anti-inflammatory. This is a single acute-exercise trial; quality read: randomized, placebo-controlled, small-sample human trial with unclear blinding.
